Chapter 17
Concerning Cruelty And Clemency, And Whether It Is Better To Be Loved Than Feared

Turning to the other qualities I mentioned earlier, I will say that every prince should want to be seen as merciful rather than cruel. However, he must be careful not to misuse this mercy. Cesare Borgia was considered cruel. Yet, his cruelty brought order to the Romagna, unified it, and restored it to peace and loyalty. If you think about it carefully, you will realize he was actually much more merciful than the people of Florence. To avoid being called cruel, the Florentines allowed the city of Pistoia to be destroyed by warring factions. Therefore, as long as a prince keeps his subjects united and loyal, he should not worry about being called cruel. By making a few harsh examples, he will ultimately be more merciful than those who are too lenient. Too much mercy allows chaos to spread, leading to murders and robberies that harm the entire community. Executions ordered by a prince, on the other hand, only harm specific individuals.

It is completely impossible for a new prince to avoid a reputation for cruelty. New states are naturally full of dangers. This is why the poet Virgil, speaking through the character of Dido, excuses the harshness of her rule by pointing out that her kingdom is new. She says that harsh necessity and the newness of her kingdom force her to do such things, and to guard her borders strictly. Still, a prince should not be too quick to believe every rumor or to take immediate action. He must not show fear. Instead, he should act calmly, using good judgment and basic humanity. Too much confidence will make him careless, and too much suspicion will make him unbearable.

This raises a famous question. Is it better to be loved than feared, or feared than loved? The answer is that a prince should want to be both. But since it is very hard to combine them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved, if you have to choose just one. You can make this general statement about human beings. They are ungrateful, fickle, fake, cowardly, and greedy. As long as you are successful, they are entirely yours. They will offer you their blood, their property, their lives, and their children, just as I said before, as long as the danger is far away. But the moment danger approaches, they will turn their backs on you. A prince who relies completely on their promises and fails to take other precautions will be ruined. Friendships bought with money, rather than earned through greatness and nobility of character, are just transactions. They are not truly secured, and you cannot rely on them when times get tough. Furthermore, people hesitate much less to betray someone they love than someone they fear. Love is held together only by a sense of obligation. Because humans are naturally selfish, they will break that bond whenever it benefits them. Fear, however, is held together by the dread of punishment, and that dread never fails you.

Even so, a prince must inspire fear in a way that avoids hatred, even if he cannot win love. It is very possible to be feared without being hated. A prince can always achieve this as long as he keeps his hands off the property and the women of his citizens and subjects. If he ever absolutely needs to execute someone, he must do it with proper justification and an obvious reason. But above all else, he must never touch anyone else's property. Men will forget the death of their father much faster than they will forget the loss of their inheritance. Besides, there is always an excuse to take someone's property. A ruler who starts living by theft will always find new reasons to seize what belongs to others. By contrast, real reasons to execute someone are harder to find and fade away much faster. However, when a prince is out with his army and in command of a massive number of soldiers, he must stop worrying completely about being called cruel. Without a reputation for cruelty, he will never be able to keep his army united and ready for action.

Historians count this among the incredible achievements of the general Hannibal. He led a massive army, made up of many different races of men, to fight in foreign lands. Yet, there was never any conflict among his men, nor did they ever rebel against him, whether he was winning or losing. This was entirely due to his inhuman cruelty. Combined with his endless abilities, this cruelty made him both deeply respected and terrifying in the eyes of his soldiers. Without that cruelty, his other great qualities would never have been enough to achieve this effect. Short-sighted writers admire his military victories on one hand, but condemn the primary cause of those victories on the other. To prove that his other virtues alone would not have been enough, just look at Scipio. Scipio was one of the greatest military commanders not just of his own time, but in all recorded history. Despite this, his own army rebelled against him in Spain. This rebellion happened for one simple reason. He was too lenient. He gave his soldiers far more freedom than is appropriate for strict military discipline. Fabius Maximus publicly scolded him for this in the Senate and literally called him the corrupter of the Roman military. Later, a governor appointed by Scipio utterly destroyed the people of Locri. Because of his easygoing nature, Scipio never avenged the victims, nor did he punish the governor's arrogance. Someone in the Senate even tried to excuse Scipio's behavior by saying that some men are much better at avoiding mistakes themselves than at correcting the mistakes of others. If Scipio had held supreme command, this soft disposition would have eventually destroyed his fame and glory. But because he operated under the strict control of the Roman Senate, this harmful character flaw was not only hidden, it actually ended up contributing to his glory.

Returning to the question of being feared or loved, I come to this conclusion. Men choose to love based on their own free will, but they fear based on the will of the prince. A wise prince should always build his foundation on what he alone controls, not on what others control. He must simply focus on making sure he avoids hatred, just as I have explained.
